title: Dig It Flat, or Build Locks and a Lake
actor_role: President of the United States; the man who must recommend one canal design to Congress
location: Washington D.C., United States (decision); Isthmus of Panama (site)
t0: In January 1906 the international Board of Consulting Engineers, convened by the Isthmian Canal Commission, hands in a split verdict: an 8-member majority recommends a sea-level canal with no locks, while a 5-member minority -- all American engineers, the report principally drafted by Henry L. Abbot -- recommends a lock-and-lake canal built around a dam across the Chagres River at Gatun. Chief Engineer John Frank Stevens, newly in the job and fresh from the excavation at Culebra, publicly sides with the minority against the board's own majority. Roosevelt must decide which design to put before Congress, which will then vote, before large-scale excavation strategy is locked in.
context_summary: Your expert board has voted 8 to 5 for a sea-level canal. Your chief engineer, who has actually walked the cut, says the minority is right and you should build locks instead. One design means digging far deeper through rock that has already defeated the French; the other means building locks and a dam bigger than anything ever attempted.
immediate_outcome: Roosevelt sent a message to Congress on February 19, 1906 endorsing the lock-and-lake design, crediting Stevens' on-the-ground judgment and the minority board members' technical case. Secretary of War William Howard Taft, forwarding both reports, had written that a sea-level canal would be preferable in principle if cost and time were no obstacle, but judged the time and cost of building one at Panama 'in effect prohibitory.' The Senate approved the lock canal on June 21, 1906 by 36 votes to 31 -- a margin showing how seriously the sea-level case was still taken.
long_term_outcome: The canal opened to traffic on August 15, 1914, using the Gatun, Pedro Miguel and Miraflores locks and Gatun Lake as planned -- and has operated for more than a century without a catastrophic lock or dam failure. The Culebra (Gaillard) Cut still had to be fought over: a major landslide in 1913 partly blocked the nearly finished channel, and slide-related widening continued for decades. The United States operated the canal until full transfer to Panama in 1999. The lock chamber dimensions fixed in 1906 eventually became a hard ceiling on ship size, and the Panama Canal Authority completed a third, larger set of locks in 2016 at a cost of roughly $5.2 billion so the canal could handle modern container ships.
uncertainty_factors: Culebra's geology known to be unstable but not quantified
Locks and dam at unprecedented scale
Cost and schedule estimates for both designs
The French failure's real cause still argued over

options.label: Sea-level canal (the board majority's recommendation)
options.short_description: One continuous channel at ocean level from coast to coast, no locks, on the Suez model -- requiring a far deeper and wider cut through the Culebra pass and some means of controlling the flooding Chagres River.
options.upside: No lock machinery to build, maintain, operate or have fail; no dependence on a single great dam whose failure could disable everything; a simpler, more permanent waterway once finished, following the prestige and precedent of Suez.
options.downside: Vastly more excavation, much of it through rock and clay at Culebra already known to slide when cut steeply -- and landslide risk grows with cut depth. Likely far more years and money than a lock canal, on ground that had already broken the French. And the Chagres would still need solving.
known_tradeoffs: Follows the world's leading precedent for an interoceanic canal and avoids betting on unprecedented lock and dam engineering; several of the board's most experienced canal engineers judged it both achievable and operationally superior in the long run. versus At the depth a sea-level design requires, Culebra could slide badly enough to block the channel repeatedly or make maintaining depth impractical -- the same failure that stopped the French at the same place.

options.label: Lock-and-lake canal (the minority's recommendation, backed by Stevens)
options.short_description: Locks lift ships to an artificial lake about 85 feet above sea level, created by damming the Chagres at Gatun, then lower them on the far side -- letting the summit level sit high and the Culebra cut stay much shallower.
options.upside: Far less excavation at Culebra, reducing though not eliminating landslide exposure; turns the Chagres from a hazard to be diverted into the water supply that fills the lake and works the locks; judged achievable on a substantially shorter schedule.
options.downside: Depends on locks and a dam at a scale with no precedent anywhere in canal engineering, introducing failure modes a sea-level channel simply would not have. Locks add operating complexity and cap the maximum ship size at the chamber dimensions -- a constraint fixed on the day the design is chosen.
known_tradeoffs: Stevens, who had seen how little decades of French and early American digging had achieved against the Culebra rock, judged a much shallower cut the only realistic route to a finished canal; the design trades excavation risk for a different but engineerable category of risk that the American minority believed could be built to a high standard. versus A lock or dam failure could disable the whole canal at a single point in a way a sea-level channel could not, and the chosen chamber size permanently caps what can pass through.

case_information.content: The Board of Consulting Engineers, convened by the Isthmian Canal Commission with both American and European members, voted 8 to 5 in its formal report to recommend a sea-level canal without locks.

The 5-member minority report -- principally drafted by retired Army engineer Henry L. Abbot and signed by Alfred Noble, Frederic P. Stearns, Joseph Ripley and Isham Randolph, all American members of the board -- recommended a lock-and-lake canal using a dam across the Chagres River at Gatun to create an elevated lake.

Chief Engineer John Frank Stevens, who had toured the excavation at Culebra and studied progress reports from the French and early American digging there, publicly sided with the lock-canal minority against the board's own majority.

A sea-level canal would require cutting a channel roughly 45 feet deeper through the Continental Divide at Culebra than a lock canal would -- far more excavation, because a lock design could hold the summit level high inside an artificial lake.

The rock and clay at Culebra were known, from French-era and ongoing American excavation, to be unstable and prone to sliding when cut into a steep, deep channel. The minority judged that a sea-level design's deeper, steeper cut carried substantially higher landslide risk than a shallower lock-canal cut. This was an engineering judgment held at the time, not a settled measurement.

The Chagres River, which crosses the canal route, floods heavily in the rainy season. A sea-level canal would have to divert or tame it to stop the channel flooding and silting; a lock-and-lake design could instead dam it at Gatun and use it as the water source for the summit lake and the locks. Both readings of the river were contemporary engineering positions.

The proposed lock canal required three sets of locks at dimensions and lift with no precedent in canal engineering anywhere in the world, plus the Gatun Dam, which would be among the largest earth dams yet attempted.

The French Panama Canal Company under Ferdinand de Lesseps had committed to a sea-level design from 1881 and collapsed in 1889 -- defeated by landslides at Culebra, cost overruns and disease among its workers -- without completing the canal.

Secretary of War William Howard Taft, forwarding both reports to Roosevelt, noted that a sea-level canal would in principle be preferable if cost and time were not obstacles, but judged the time and cost of building one at Panama 'in effect prohibitory.'

Advocates of the sea-level design argued it needed no lock machinery that could fail or be sabotaged, put no dependence on a single dam whose failure could be catastrophic, and offered simpler and more permanent operation once built -- following the precedent and prestige of the sea-level Suez Canal.
The lock canal as actually built would perform successfully through the rest of the twentieth century and beyond, carrying growing volumes of shipping without a catastrophic lock or dam failure.

By the late twentieth and early twenty-first century, container ships would outgrow the original 1914 lock chambers (roughly 305 by 33.5 metres), forcing Panama to build an entirely new, larger third set of locks -- completed in 2016 at a cost of roughly $5.2 billion -- to stay competitive for the largest modern vessels.

Even the shallower lock-canal cut would still demand heavy excavation and repeated widening at Culebra, including a major landslide in 1913 that partly blocked the nearly finished channel before opening, and slide-related maintenance for decades after.

Stevens, despite winning the design argument and organising the construction effort, would resign in February 1907 -- a year after this decision and well before the excavation was finished. Historians still differ on why.

evidence.citation: Recorded rather than resolved; see the discussion of each point.
evidence.supported_claim: Two points are not settled. First, sources agree on the 8-5 vote and on the five named American minority members, but differ on how precisely to characterise the majority's composition; the common claim that the sea-level majority was dominated by the board's European members is treated here as a secondary, less rigorously sourced detail rather than an established fact. Second, historians differ on why Stevens resigned in February 1907 -- explanations range from the pressure of the job to friction with Washington to personal and financial motives -- and no single account is treated here as settled.
